analysis.one_liner: Expanded health coverage subsidies, closed the Medicare drug coverage gap, and switched student loans from private banks to direct federal lending, funded by a tax on investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill passed both chambers along party lines and was signed March 30, 2010, becoming Public Law 111-152.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill fixed up the main health care law passed three days earlier: bigger tax credits to help families afford insurance, better coverage inside the Medicare drug plan's 'donut hole', higher federal payments to states for Medicaid, and extra funding for community health centers. It also ended the decades-old system where private banks received federal subsidies to issue student loans, moving all loans to direct federal lending and using the savings for larger Pell Grants and easier loan repayment. It raised the money through taxes, including a new 3.8% tax on investment income for households making over $200,000 ($250,000 married).
analysis.who_benefits: Families with incomes up to 400% of the poverty line get larger premium tax credits and richer cost-sharing help; Medicare Part D enrollees get a $250 rebate and coverage in the donut hole reaching 75% discounts by 2020; low-income Medicare beneficiaries get simplified financial assistance; primary care physicians see Medicaid rates rise to Medicare levels for 2013-2014 with full federal funding; states get higher Medicaid matching rates (100% in 2014-2016); territories get increased Medicaid funding and an Exchange option; community health centers, nursing workforce programs, and Pell Grant recipients benefit; student borrowers gain income-based repayment capped at 10% of discretionary income and forgiveness after 20 years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured families, Medicare drug enrollees, students, health centers

how_it_helps.text: Bigger premium tax credits: a sliding scale applies for household incomes up to 400% of poverty, with a failsafe to keep spending below 0.504% of GDP if premiums outgrow incomes
Cost-sharing protections strengthened for low- and middle-income insureds (94%, 87%, 73%, 70% actuarial value tiers replacing 90%/80%)
Medicare Part D enrollees who hit the coverage gap in 2010 receive a one-time $250 rebate, and by 2020 the donut hole is closed with 75% discounts on brand-name and generic drugs
Medicaid expansion funding set at 100% federal match for 2014-2016, 95% in 2017, 94% in 2018, 93% in 2019, and 90% after, with extra transitional help for expansion states covering childless adults
Medicaid payment rates for primary care physicians raised to at least 100% of Medicare rates for 2013-2014, fully federally funded

All new student loans move to the Direct Loan program after June 2010; income-based repayment lowered to 10% of discretionary income with forgiveness after 20 years for new borrowers after July 2014; Pell Grants fully funded
Insurance reforms applied to grandfathered plans: no lifetime limits, restricted rescissions, dependent coverage to age 26, no preexisting-condition exclusions by 2014
Community health centers receive enhanced FY2011-FY2015 funding; historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions funded through FY2019

Community mental health centers must provide at least 40% of services to non-Medicare beneficiaries; Medicare prepayment review limits repealed; extra funding appropriated to fight fraud, waste, and abuse
A 3.8% tax on net investment income for taxpayers with AGI over $200,000 ($250,000 joint), starting in 2013
Economic substance doctrine codified with penalties, targeting transactions lacking business purpose
Territories (Puerto Rico, Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, Northern Marianas) gain higher Medicaid caps and may elect to run a Health Benefits Exchange

analysis.who_pays: Wealthier households pay a new 3.8% tax on investment income above $200,000/$250,000 AGI; large corporations pay a one-time 15.75% increase in Q3 2014 estimated tax payments; medical device manufacturers pay a new 2.3% excise tax on sales after 2012; health insurers pay delayed fees on net premium income (to 2014); brand-name drug makers face delayed fees (to 2011) and delayed loss of the Part D subsidy deduction (to 2013); new line-extension drugs owe higher Medicaid rebates; employers with 50+ employees face a $2,000 per-employee penalty (first 30 exempted) for not offering coverage, plus more stringent Medicare Advantage benchmarks and payment updates for hospitals and imaging; cellulosic biofuel producers see credit restrictions.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, large corporations, drug/device/insurer industries

drawbacks.text: The employer penalty rises to $2,000 per employee beyond the first 30, potentially discouraging hiring at the margin for firms near the threshold, and the individual mandate penalties (2.5% of income over the filing threshold, capped at $695 by 2016) impose real costs on people who remain uncovered
Medicare Advantage benchmarks are reduced (95%-115% of fee-for-service) and frozen in 2011, cutting payments to private Medicare plans that many seniors use
Medicaid disproportionate share hospital payments are cut beginning in 2014 (aggregate reductions reaching $5.6 billion by 2019), reducing funds safety-net hospitals rely on to treat the uninsured

Payments to inpatient, long-term care, rehabilitation, psychiatric, and outpatient hospitals are reduced through lower market-basket updates for FY2014-2019, which could pressure rural and safety-net facilities

The high-cost employer plan ('Cadillac') excise tax is only delayed to 2018 with higher thresholds ($10,200/$27,500), leaving a future tax on generous employer plans that could eventually hit union and middle-class health benefits

The community health center and community college funding relies on authorizations, which depend on later appropriations; the Education and Labor provisions carry out student loan savings while nonprofit servicers get guaranteed allocations (100,000 borrower accounts each) and payments to retain FFEL-era jobs, blunting some savings

Closing the donut hole and expanding Medicaid impose new obligations on drug makers (delayed fees, higher line-extension rebates) that could be passed to consumers through higher prices, and the generic-gap coinsurance falls only gradually to 25% by 2020

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits—expanded coverage subsidies, donut-hole relief, stronger Medicaid funding, and student loan relief—are substantial and broadly targeted at low- and middle-income people, and they are paid for by redirecting bank subsidies and by taxes concentrated on high earners, large corporations, and health industry fees. The main costs are borne by Medicare Advantage plans, safety-net hospitals, and the health industry, with a risk that some industry fees and hospital cuts pass through to consumers. The individual mandate penalty is a real cost on the uninsured, though the employer penalty exemption for the first 30 workers and the 2018 delay on the high-cost plan tax soften some burdens. On balance, the transfer flows toward ordinary people, but hospital and DSH cuts create genuine hardship risk in areas where coverage expansion lags.

outcome.mechanism: Passed the House 220-211 on March 21, passed the Senate 56-43 on March 25 (under a budget-reconciliation process allowing a majority vote), then the House accepted the Senate's changes 220-207 the same day, and the President signed it March 30, 2010.

narrative.text: Introduced March 17, 2010, reported same day by the House Budget Committee as an original measure, placed on the Union Calendar, and brought to the floor under a closed rule with no amendments allowed
An attempt to recommit with instructions to the Budget Committee (Rep. Camp, R-MI) failed 199-232, with all 178 Republicans voting yes and 21 Democrats crossing over
Passed the House 220-211; all 178 Republicans voted no, and 33 Democrats voted no as well

In the Senate, a motion to proceed agreed to 56-40 on March 23; multiple motions by Republican senators (Crapo, Enzi, Hatch, Cornyn, Roberts, Alexander, DeMint) to send the bill to committees were all tabled on mostly party-line votes (56-43, 58-41, 52-46, 59-37)

A budget point of order under Section 313(b)(1)(a) of the Congressional Budget Act (Byrd Rule) against provisions at pages 118 and 120 was raised and sustained on March 25, striking those provisions before final passage
The Senate passed the bill 56-43 on March 25; all 40 voting Republicans were opposed, while 3 Senate Democrats also voted no
The House agreed to the Senate's amendments 220-207 on March 25 (220 of 253 Democrats voting yes; no Republicans in favor)
Signed by the President on March 30, 2010; became Public Law 111-152

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uninsured families, Medicare drug enrollees facing the donut hole, student borrowers, community health centers, and hospitals serving high Medicaid volumes came out ahead. The industries that lost are private Medicare Advantage plans, for-profit student loan companies losing their federal lending role, and drug/medical device makers facing new taxes and rebates. High-income households ($200,000+ AGI) bear a new investment income tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Uninsured families, Medicare drug enrollees, student borrowers

sides.party_line_note: The vote was sharply partisan: every House Republican and 40 of 41 Senate Republicans opposed the bill, while roughly 87% of House Democrats (220 of 253) and all but 3 Senate Democrats supported it, with a handful of Democrats in both chambers defecting.

industries.industry: Private student loan companies (FFEL program lenders)
industries.note: The bill ends new FFEL loans after June 2010, shutting off a federal-subsidized private lending channel; nonprofit servicers receive guaranteed allocations and payments to retain FFEL-era jobs, softening the blow for those, but the for-profit middleman role is eliminated. Ordinary borrowers gain simpler direct loans and better repayment terms.

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage plans (private insurers in Medicare)
industries.note: Payment benchmarks are cut and frozen in 2011, with a medical loss ratio requirement (at least 85%) or the plan must remit money to the government; plans can be barred from new enrollment and terminated if the MLR fails for five years. This reduces plan profitability and may lead to reduced plan choices or benefits for seniors enrolled in MA plans.

The bill requires manufacturer participation in the donut-hole discount program (delayed to 2011) and delays the branded prescription drug fee and Part D subsidy deduction elimination, while also requiring higher rebates on new line-extension drugs. These changes cut into industry revenue but also secure industry's central role in Medicare drug pricing going forward.

A new 2.3% excise tax applies to sales after 2012 on devices other than retail items like eyeglasses, contacts, and hearing aids, raising costs for the industry and potentially for consumers as costs pass through.

The net premium income fee is delayed to 2014, and grandfathered plans must comply with new insurance reforms (no lifetime limits, age-26 dependent coverage, no preexisting-condition exclusions by 2014). The bill entrenches the private insurance model (Exchanges, grandfathered plans) while adding new rules and a fee.
A one-time 15.75% increase in Q3 2014 estimated tax payments raises revenue from the largest firms; this is a timing-based tax rather than a permanent rate increase.

industries.industry: Hospitals (inpatient, long-term care, rehabilitation, psychiatric, outpatient)
industries.note: Market-basket updates are reduced for FY2014-2019, Medicaid and Medicare DSH payments are cut (aggregate Medicaid DSH reductions reaching $5.6 billion by 2019), and imaging payment rules change. Hospitals gain indirectly from more insured patients under the ACA's Medicaid expansion and exchange subsidies, but the payment cuts are real revenue losses, particularly for safety-net institutions.

The effective date for the physician-ownership ban is postponed to December 31, 2010 for existing facilities, with exceptions for high-Medicaid hospitals; expansion limitations on operating rooms and beds are modified rather than eliminated, preserving some physician self-referral revenue.

industries.industry: Community mental health centers serving Medicare patients
industries.note: New requirements (at least 40% non-Medicare service share, no in-home/inpatient/residential partial hospitalization) tighten a channel some centers used for Medicare revenue.
A new 3.8% tax on net investment income begins in 2013, the largest single revenue source in the bill; this is a direct tax on wealth rather than a spending cut elsewhere.

Economic substance doctrine codified with penalties, targeting transactions with no business purpose; corporate estimated tax payments for large firms accelerated. These are modest but real constraints on aggressive tax planning.
